extraction.research_question: Does firms' lobbying causally increase firm size, and how much does lobbying reduce aggregate productivity through misallocation of resources across firms (distortion of firm size)? (Abstract; Introduction, printed pp.1-3)
extraction.theory: Heterogeneous-firm general-equilibrium model with endogenous lobbying, extending Hsieh and Klenow (2009) along Melitz (2003) lines. Firms differ in productivity, lobbying productivity and an exogenous wedge; a fixed lobbying cost induces selection into lobbying; lobbying yields output distortions tau_s(phi) that raise a lobbying firm's revenue (eq. 1, p.14). Microfoundation (Section 3.2, pp.18-20): a three-stage game in which the government's welfare combines household utility with a CES aggregate of lobbying expenditure (a generalization of Grossman and Helpman 1994). Stated rationale for heterogeneous distortions: the government's "love for variety" in lobbying reduces political risk from concentrated influence (p.20). Proposition 3 (p.20): distortions rise with the mass of lobbying firms and fall with the lobbying elasticity sigma_L.
extraction.data: Lobbying: parsed LD-1 and LD-2 Lobbying Disclosure Act reports from the Senate Office of Public Records, 1999-2015 filings (Appendix A, printed p.38); 972,005 report-level observations after dropping amendments. More than one million original filings were parsed (p.4). Client names linked to Compustat gvkeys: 67,842 unique client names (p.5). Bills and committees: 65,047 lobbied bills across the 106th-115th Congresses (Figure 5; the 1,862 trade bills are a subset); committee assignments from Stewart and Woon (2011). Firm sample: all US publicly traded firms in Compustat, 1999-2018 (p.4-5). Unit: firm-year (Table 2 regressions). Regression N for log sales: 15,332 (all years) and 8,796 (post-2007); profits: 10,369 and 6,064; value added (Table F.2): 10,851 and 6,097. Industry data: BEA value-added, labor, and intermediate input shares for 2000-2017 (Figures 8-11). Campaign contributions: FEC data (Figure 1). Financial variables are described only as standard characteristics of public firms (the source database is not named in the extracted text).
extraction.method: Descriptive stylized facts (Section 2); OLS and IV panel regressions of log sales and log profits on log lobbying expenditure with firm, year and state-year fixed effects, standard errors double-clustered by firm and year (Table 2, Appendix F); structural model estimated by simulated method of moments (nine parameters: production and lobbying fixed costs, variances and covariances of productivity and wedge, and beta), with sigma_C=4, death rate 0.025 and beta_s=beta imposed (pp.27-31); counterfactual with beta=0 and a sensitivity sweep over sigma_C (pp.31-32). The SMM text says the weighting matrix is the generalized inverse of the moment covariance, but for now it uses the identity matrix (fn.22, p.29).
extraction.identification: Shift-share instrument (eq. 12, p.21): z_it = sum over politicians j in firm i's connections of [sum over committees c of w_ict-k * d_jct]. Share w_ict-k = firm i's share of lobbied bills assigned to committee c, lagged (preferred t-1; t-2 and t-3 in Tables F.1-F.2). Shift d_jct = indicator that politician j sits on committee c in year t. Connections = politicians representing the state of the firm's headquarters. Identifying assumption: committee moves by politicians are exogenous to firm characteristics and influence (p.22). Relevance: 30 percent average probability a politician changes committee between Congresses (p.22; about 29 percent in Figure C.2).
extraction.scope: Population: US publicly traded firms in Compustat (1999-2018) and lobbying clients of federal lobbying disclosure filings. Institution: US federal lobbying under the Lobbying Disclosure Act of 1995 and congressional standing committees (Table C.2; Figure 6 and C.1 show senators, 106th-115th Congresses). Era: 1999-2018. Model economy: multi-industry US economy with 17 industries (Figures 8-11).

limitations: Identification depends on committee-membership moves being exogenous to firms. The authors concede politicians may choose committees to deliver targeted benefits to connected firms (printed p.26) and that committee weights could reflect anticipated changes (tested with a near-zero correlation, p.25).
Headquarters are assumed fixed; the authors report no headquarter changes in their data, and a politician changing district has under 1 percent probability (p.24-25).
The instrument's relevance is modest: first-stage F is 13-14 in the preferred specifications and falls to 6-10 with t-2 or t-3 weights (Tables 2, F.1, F.2).
Headline 3 percent versus preferred-column 0.2 percent inconsistency (see key findings); the text's claim of an order-of-magnitude IV-OLS gap does not match Table 2 (about 4.5 to 7 times).

Elasticity of substitution sigma_C is not estimated; it is fixed at 4 for lack of data, and the paper acknowledges results depend on it (p.27, p.32). Industry-specific beta_s and sigma_C are restricted to be common across industries (p.27).

Model is simplified: one industry and one factor for exposition (fn.14); demand shifters ignored (fn.9); extensions to decreasing returns and demand shifters deferred to future versions (fn.10); Hsieh-Klenow caveats (Haltiwanger et al. 2018) noted but not addressed; the counterfactual uses aggregate productivity, not output, because there is no capital or human capital accumulation (fn.23). The analysis is partial equilibrium except for the Section 4.2 general-equilibrium counterfactual (fn.13).

Lobbying-to-distortion mapping is assumed in Section 3.1 and microfounded only through a government welfare function whose lobbying-income motive is not justified (p.19-20, fn.15). Equation (10) assumes truth-telling, and coordination issues are set aside as beyond scope (p.19).
SMM uses an identity weighting matrix for the baseline, despite the stated generalized-inverse weighting (fn.22, p.29).

Lobbying amounts are self-reported estimates rounded to the nearest $5,000 (pre-2008 larger rounding bins; Appendix A, fn.25). Client-name matching is algorithmic plus manual, validated on a 5 percent random sample (Appendix A, fn.27-28, printed p.38-39).
Date inconsistency: the data are described as covering 1999-2018 (Introduction), but Appendix A says LD-1 and LD-2 filings from 1999-2015 were used.
The persistence measure is conservative (two adjacent years only), and the persistence drops during the 2007-2009 crisis (p.10).
Open questions the authors leave: why entry into lobbying is limited, why persistence is high, the reverse effect of size on lobbying, and business-cycle effects (p.33).

summary_md:
Huneeus and Kim link federal LDA lobbying reports (1999-2015 filings, about 972k report rows) to US public firms in Compustat. They ask two questions: does lobbying make a firm bigger, and what does that cost the economy in productivity?

**Descriptive facts**
- Lobbying is rare: 766 of 7,646 public firms lobbied in 2017.
- It is very persistent: more than 80% of 2016 lobbyists lobbied again in 2017, with an intensive-margin slope of 0.922.
- It runs to more than 6 times PAC-type campaign contributions.
- Most bills draw a median of 2 lobbying clients.

**Causal estimate.** The instrument is a shift-share. For each firm it combines its lagged share of lobbied bills going to each committee with the committee seats held by politicians from its headquarters state. The IV elasticity of sales on lobbying is 0.319 for all years (first-stage F 14.3) and 0.227 after 2007 (F 13.1). OLS gives about 0.04-0.05. The paper's "3 percent per 10 percent" headline uses the full-sample estimate, while its stated preferred estimate is 0.2 percent per 1 percent.

**Structural model.** A Hsieh-Klenow/Melitz model is fitted by SMM with an identity weighting matrix. With sigma_C fixed at 4, removing the return to lobbying raises aggregate productivity by 22%. That figure moves from 38% to 13% as sigma_C goes from 2 to 6.

**What it means for Paul's systems.** Nothing here estimates how a member of Congress responds to money. The usable pieces are narrower:
- The committee-relevance weight is computed from data, where the committee pillar's tier weights are owner judgment.
- The persistence facts explain why naive carry-forward is hard to beat in Mentat's lobbying forecasts.
- The paper's causal direction (lobbying leads to revenue) is a simultaneity warning for the sector-growth study's growth-leads-to-lobbying regressions.
- Appendix A's fuzzy matching with a 5% random validation sample is a template for auditing the LDA client classifier.

All transfers are UNVERIFIED (DE-062) until a second path reproduces them.

extraction.title: Measuring Politicians' Public Personality Traits Using Computational Text Analysis: A Multimethod Feasibility Study for Agency and Communion
extraction.venue: Political Analysis (2025), 00, 1-19 (received 20 April 2025; revised 23 September 2025; accepted 23 September 2025)
extraction.document_type: Journal article: empirical measurement and computational text-analysis validation (feasibility study)
extraction.coverage: Full text read in both chunks: all 1,044 lines of the text file (pp. 1-19, including the references and cite block). Nothing skipped. Metadata hint confirmed: authors, venue, year and DOI match; the header says "Multimethod" and the data statement and reference list say "Multi-Method", so no correction is needed. Annotations: both JSON files read in full. 227050d08dac.json has 80 items (79 highlights plus one line on p.10). d71ad6e32e9a.json repeats the same markup on the same spans, with variant span boundaries and mixed colors, plus one extra highlight on p.1 ("less attention has been given to the traits politicians project..."). paul_markup below lists the 80 items from the first file plus that one extra item, 81 in all. Every content field in both files is empty, so there is no sticky-note text. Colors (yellow, green, pink, purple in the second file) have no legend and no meaning is inferred. The Supplementary Material (Appendices A-N: codebook, prompts, hyperparameters, test-unit list, partisan and gender tables) is cited but not in the text file, so those details are unverified. Scope note: the paper has no content on networks, lobbying, path-finding, allocation or election outcomes beyond citing personality-election links in the literature review.
extraction.research_question: Can computational text analysis validly measure politicians' public personality, operationalized as the agency and communion traits they project in speeches, interviews and social media posts? Which measurement strategy (supervised SVM, fine-tuned XLM-RoBERTa, or zero/few-shot prompting of generative LLMs) yields the most valid measure? (Sections 1 and 3.)
extraction.theory: Brunswik (1952) lens model (Fig. 1): observers never see intrinsic personality (Y_IPT) directly; they infer it from observable personality cues X1...Xn, which are shaped by intrinsic personality and by strategic self-presentation (Y_S) (Sec. 2.2, p.3). Two problems follow: cue validity (traits are fuzzy, and some are hard to observe) and cue utilization (behaviors are equifinal/multifinal and viewers' partisan biases shape interpretation) (Sec. 2.3, pp.3-4). Trait choice: agency and communion as "meta-traits" (Bakan 1966; Hogan 1982: "get ahead" vs "get along") (Sec. 3.2.1.1, p.7). Operational definitions come from the Lechner et al. (2025) PoliPers domain-specific politician framework (15 facets): agency = Assertiveness & Will to Take Control; communion = Empathy & Compassion, positive poles only (p.7). Strong cues are direct self-statements; weak cues are indirect (p.7). Background: candidate-centered personalization (McAllister 2007; Pedersen and Rahat 2021) and congruency/heuristic accounts of voter preference (Caprara and Zimbardo 2004) (Sec. 2.1, p.3).
extraction.data: Corpus: 46 leading German politicians (leaders or co-leaders of party and/or parliamentary-group, covering all six Bundestag parties; list in Supplementary App. A), 2017-2024, spanning two full Bundestag terms (Sec. 3.1, p.5). Three sources: (1) 99 interviews with political leaders in five broadcast formats (PolInterviews dataset; Birkenmaier, Sieber and Bergstein 2025) (p.5); (2) a 300,000-post subsample of Facebook posts drawn from a raw corpus of 6.7 million politician posts (p.6); (3) German Bundestag speeches from the ParlSpeech V2 German subset (Rauh and Schwalbach 2020) (p.6). Unit of analysis: individual sentences/statements. Main corpus: a random sample of 15,000 sentences per source, so 45,000 sentences in total (implied; the text does not state the total) (p.6). Human annotation: 1,000 sentences coded by three annotators (the first author and two RAs) for agreement; a human-labeled corpus with at least 200 examples per class (agency, communion, none) for weak and strong cues (pp.7-8). Classifier evaluation set: the Fig. 3 caption reports n = 600 (balanced and unbalanced); the split is not described further in the text (p.10). Functional test set: 18 units (p.11). Partisan validation: party-level CHES expert positions (Jolly et al. 2022) for the full unlabeled corpus. US debate: transcripts of the 10 September 2024 Trump-Harris debate from the American Presidency Project, machine-translated EN to DE with the DeepL API; Trump n = 655 utterances, Harris n = 320 (p.13).
extraction.method: Measurement workflow (Fig. 2, p.6): codebook development and manual coding, then computational classification with three strategies, then validation under the ValiText framework (Birkenmaier, Wagner and Lechner 2024). Labels: agency / communion / none, with a one-sentence rationale per prediction for prompting (p.8). Strategy 1 (supervised): linear SVM on bag-of-words, following Ramey et al. (2019), with fivefold cross-validation and 80/20 splits (p.8). Strategy 2 (semisupervised): fine-tuned XLM-RoBERTa base (279M parameters), threefold CV with 80/20 splits (p.8). Strategy 3 (prompting, no training): GPT-4o (proprietary), Llama 3-8B and DeepSeek-V3, each zero-shot and few-shot, with templates tailored to strong-only vs strong+weak datasets (pp.8-9). Dataset variants: strong-only vs weak+strong; balanced vs unbalanced (where "none" is twice as frequent as each trait class) (p.8). Each model run with three random seeds; metric is macro-F1 averaged across runs (pp.9-10). Validation: (a) agreement with the human test set (macro-F1; Krippendorff's alpha for human coders); (b) structural/functional tests on 18 units (6 self-report items from the Lechner et al. inventory, 6 opposing-pole items expected to be "other", 6 unrelated corpus sentences expected to be "other"); (c) sensitivity to partisan variation using party CHES positions and the debate. Results are reported only for DeepSeek-V3 in the partisan section because it was the only model to pass all earlier steps (p.12).
extraction.identification: No causal identification strategy. Validity is argued through convergence with human labels (macro-F1), structural functional tests, and expected correlations with ideology (CHES) and with the 2024 debate's widely reported Trump/Harris contrast (Hyatt et al. 2018). The authors state that the relative weight of intrinsic personality and strategic self-presentation in any cue cannot be determined, and say this does not matter because the goal is to automate the judgments the public would form from the cues (Sec. 2.2, p.3).
extraction.scope: Population: 46 leading German politicians (all six Bundestag parties) plus two US presidential-debate candidates. Institutions: German Bundestag (speeches and interviews) and social media. Era: 2017-2024 for German data; one debate on 10 September 2024. Language: German (the US debate was translated). Unit: sentence. Traits: only agency and communion, verbal cues only (no paraverbal, nonverbal or video). Authors position it as a feasibility and measurement-validation study, not a substantive test of drivers of personality change.

key_findings.finding: Prompt-based classification with DeepSeek-V3 is the best-performing strategy on the human-labeled test data; GPT-4o is close behind. Macro-F1 is about 0.74-0.77 across the top configurations.
key_findings.numbers: DeepSeek-V3 few-shot, strong, balanced: 0.77 (SD 0.02); DeepSeek-V3 few-shot, weak+strong, balanced: 0.76 (SD 0.01); GPT-4o few-shot, strong, balanced: 0.76 (SD 0.01); DeepSeek-V3 few-shot, strong, unbalanced: 0.77 (SD 0.01); GPT-4o few-shot, strong, unbalanced: 0.74 (SD 0.00); DeepSeek-V3 zero-shot, strong, unbalanced: 0.74 (SD 0.01)

key_findings.finding: Supervised and semisupervised baselines underperform. The SVM is best on strong balanced data; XLM-RoBERTa is best overall among the non-prompting methods. Llama 3-8B is weakest and most variable across runs.
key_findings.numbers: SVM: F1 0.63 strong balanced (large SD), 0.59 weak+strong balanced, 0.55 and 0.61 on the two unbalanced sets. XLM-RoBERTa: 0.70 strong balanced (best non-prompt result). Llama 3-8B: about 0.60 balanced and 0.55 unbalanced.

key_findings.finding: No model exceeds macro-F1 0.80. Human agreement is moderate.
key_findings.location: Sec. 4.1 and Sec. 5, p.9 and p.14; Table 1, p.10
key_findings.numbers: Krippendorff's alpha for cue presence: .73 strong, .72 weak+strong. Agency alpha .70 (strong) and .71 (weak+strong); communion .78 and .74.

key_findings.finding: Human coders mostly label sentences as no cue. Among cue sentences, communion is more common than agency.

key_findings.numbers: Communion share by party: LINKE 19%, Greens 12%, SPD 10%, CDU 8%, AfD and FDP about 6% each. The text reports regression lines and standard-error bars but no coefficients, N or CIs in the main text.

key_findings.finding: Agency at party level has only a weak positive link with the economic CHES dimension and none with the cultural dimension (footnote, Appendix L).
key_findings.numbers: No coefficient reported in the main text.

key_findings.finding: In the 2024 debate the measure separates the two candidates as expected: Harris shows more personality cues overall, and the agency/communion balance reverses between them.
key_findings.numbers: Personality-cue share: Harris about 23%, Trump about 10%. Trump: 63% agency / 37% communion. Harris: 59% communion / 41% agency. Utterances: Trump 655, Harris 320.

key_findings.finding: Communion is higher on social media than in interviews; agency varies less across sources. Female politicians show higher communion.
key_findings.numbers: No values reported in the main text.

key_findings.finding: Validity claim summary: prompt-based methods, particularly GPT-4o and DeepSeek-V3, allow the most valid measurement; strong-only cue definitions perform better than weak+strong.
key_findings.numbers: Strong-only definitions performed better, as the authors expected; no delta is reported in the main text.

limitations: Only two traits (agency and communion) are measured; the authors call for expanding to other traits (p.15).
Verbal cues only; paraverbal and nonverbal cues (rhetoric, gesture, video, audio) are excluded; future work should be multimodal (p.15).
Sentence-level analysis only; paragraph- or token-level extensions are suggested (p.15).
Human agreement is moderate (alpha .70-.78), and no computational model exceeds macro-F1 0.80, so the ceiling on measurement precision is set by fuzzy constructs (pp.14-15).

LLM bias: generative models may reflect pretraining biases. The authors report no systematic bias in their checks but cite reports of pro-Chinese bias in DeepSeek models (Huang et al. 2025) and recommend extra validation for politically sensitive content (p.15).
Small functional-test set (n = 18) and a small debate comparison (two speakers, translated transcripts) (pp.11-13).
Partisan validation is descriptive at party level in the main text, with no reported inferential statistics; the Chapel Hill comparison relies on six parties (pp.12-13).

Self-report personality inventories are argued to be susceptible to social desirability (footnote 3, p.4); the paper treats politicians' self-reports as a kind of self-statement cue rather than intrinsic traits.
Supplementary appendices (codebook, prompts, hyperparameters, extra partisan and gender analyses) are not in the text file reviewed here, so they are unverified.
Feasibility scope: the paper argues feasibility and does not test explanatory factors for changes in displayed personality (crisis events, role transitions), which it proposes as future work (p.14).

summary_md:
Birkenmaier and Lechner ask whether a politician's *public* personality, meaning the traits they project rather than their intrinsic traits, can be measured from text. They use Brunswik's lens model: observers only ever see cues, and those cues mix true personality with strategic self-presentation. The operational definitions come from the PoliPers framework. Agency is Assertiveness & Will to Take Control. Communion is Empathy & Compassion. Only the positive poles count, and cues are split into strong and weak.

The data are 45,000 German sentences, 15,000 each from Bundestag speeches, broadcast interviews and Facebook posts, covering 46 party leaders from 2017 to 2024. Few-shot prompting of DeepSeek-V3 and GPT-4o reaches macro-F1 0.74-0.77. Fine-tuned XLM-R reaches 0.70, bag-of-words SVM 0.55-0.63, and Llama 3-8B about 0.55-0.60. Human coders agree only moderately (alpha 0.70-0.78), and coders label 89-94% of sentences as having no cue. Strong-only definitions work better than strong plus weak. Only GPT-4o and DeepSeek pass the 18-unit functional test.

For external validity, communion share falls from left to right (LINKE 19% down to AfD and FDP about 6%). In the 2024 debate, Trump's cues were 63% agency and Harris's were 59% communion.

For Melange, this paper is the direct method source for `fec/members/agency_communion_llm.py`. That file copies the codebook, the positive-pole rule and the 18-unit test, and it reproduces the left-greater-than-right communion pattern (D .099 vs R .049). But the build departs from the paper in ways that matter:
- It uses a different model family (Claude Sonnet, in English).
- It keeps weak cues in the score.
- It samples only self-referential floor and hearing sentences, 40 per member.
- It has no human-labelled macro-F1 test set.

The paper says nothing to support the next step the system takes: turning projected persona into susceptibility to lobbying pressure. That mapping (.60 z(communion) − .40 z(agency) in the receptivity layer) is a design prior. Its one behavioural test so far (H4, +0.067 on Nokken-Poole drift) is below the threshold. The paper also gently undercuts the Ramey/Mairesse lexical lineage behind the Big Five reader.

summary_issues: Overall: no bearing is refuted outright. Three are reproduced on the paper side (party gradient, receptivity-layer scope, stance ordering), and five are softened for overstatement or wrong attribution.

Functional test overstated: GPT-4o classifies all 18 units only on strong labels. On weak plus strong labels only DeepSeek-V3 does (paper Sec 4.3 p.12). The summary sentence 'Only GPT-4o and DeepSeek pass the 18-unit functional test' should say so.

Debate figures lack a denominator and window. The 63/37 and 59/41 agency-communion splits are shares of personality-cue sentences for each candidate. Cue shares are about 23 percent (Harris) and 10 percent (Trump) of utterances; n is 655 (Trump) and 320 (Harris). One debate, 10 Sep 2024, machine-translated from English to German with DeepL.
The 45,000 total sentences is implied (15,000 per source, three sources). The paper never states the total; the summary presents it as fact.

Paul attribution unsupported: every paul_markup note in the item is blank and paul_entries has no takeaways. The quoted phrase 'bag-of-words SVM baselines outdated' is the paper's own wording about Ramey (p.5), not a Paul note. The claims about Paul endorsing LLM readers, the gold-panel note and the stance SVM annotation need a source or should be removed.

Corpus description is off: agency_communion_llm.py queries the whole speeches table with a self-reference filter (lines 127-138). It does not restrict to floor and hearing speech. The big5 comment says that table holds CREC, INTERVIEW and legacy CHRG rows.
The Pink reader is called 'holistic' Big Five items. big5_llm.py is item-level by design (20 IPIP-style items, 4 per trait).

The Mairesse SMOreg description conflicts with big5_traits.py, whose header says published standardized correlates were used as linear weights, not the Mairesse model. The brain says the refit weights are saved as mairesse_smoreg.json.

Ramey citation year: the paper's reference list gives Ramey, Klingler and Hollibaugh 2019, PSRM 7(1): 163-184. The item, the code header and the brain all say 2016. The item metadata should be reconciled.

Amsalem link dropped: the paper cites Amsalem et al. 2020, 'Fine-Grained Analysis of Diversity Levels in the News', for media visibility, not the 2018 personality paper in the research vault. The 'cites' relation was therefore unsupported and the item is not in the related list.
Byrne, Ornstein, Mondak and Koutsoumpis are not cited by the paper. The rel wording implies the paper points to them; their links are the analyst's additions and are labelled complements.

Paper-internal rounding: Sec 4.1 p.9 gives 63 percent communion and 38 percent agency for weak plus strong cues, which sum to 101 percent. Flag as a paper-side inconsistency; it does not change any bearing.

Brain-sourced figures were not rechecked against data: party signature D .099 vs R .049; H4 +0.067 against a 0.094 floor; Pink diagonal +0.064 against a 0.12 bar (0.12 not located); mean held-out r 0.350; stance 83.9 percent, 0.816 and 0.757.
Strong-only superiority: the paper reports no delta, and the Table 2 gap is 0.01 within SD (see the qualifies bearing on strong-only).
The code docstring (agency_communion_llm.py lines 7-8) says the paper's comparator is fine-tuned RoBERTa. The paper uses XLM-RoBERTa. This is a code-side wording nit.
gaps_exposed: The English Claude agency/communion instrument has no human-labelled sentence test set (3 coders, codebook, Krippendorff alpha, macro-F1). Only the 18-unit functional gate and the party signature are reproduced, so the paper's 0.74-0.77 cannot be claimed for this model.
No strong-only variant has been computed, although the paper found strong-only definitions more valid. The cache holds strength labels, so this costs nothing to compute.

Persona comes only from the speeches table (floor and hearings), with self-referential filtering and 40 sentences per member. The paper shows communion differs by source (higher on social media), and the system has no per-genre persona estimate.

persona_susc_z is z-scored across parties together (receptivity_layer.py:152-155), even though both the paper and the system show a party gap in communion. There is no within-party standardization and no sex control (the paper reports higher communion for female politicians).
Persona is a static snapshot. The paper flags role transitions (becoming chair or lead candidate) and crises as drivers of displayed personality, and no time window or change tracking exists.

There is no audit for partisan or pretraining bias in the LLM classifier, which the paper recommends for political content. The party signature alone cannot separate a real party difference from model bias.
flags: UNSTRATIFIED: persona_susc_z pools D and R in its z-scores (fec/members/receptivity_layer.py:152-155) across a fault line that both the paper and the system's own party signature (D .099 vs R .049) show. Any figure quoting a persona effect must carry the UNSTRATIFIED label or be split by party.

Attribution overreach in code comments: receptivity_layer.py:140-142 cites the Birkenmaier-Lechner cue shares and gives the communion→susceptible and agency→resistant mapping in the same comment. The paper makes no claim about susceptibility or pressure response, so the mapping should be attributed to Byrne-style design priors.

Model mismatch: the paper validated GPT-4o and DeepSeek-V3. The system runs Claude sonnet-5 or fable (agency_communion_llm.py:24). 'Instrument replicates the paper' (brain line 55) should be scoped to the functional gate and the party-direction signature only.

PERSONA_W 0.30 is a standing owner ruling (do not propose removal). Nothing in this paper is offered as grounds to remove it. Behavioural validity of the channel is still unverified (H4 +0.067, below the floor).

Paul's annotation on the supervised stance stack ('bag-of-words SVM baselines outdated') conflicts with the system's in-domain held-out result: LinearSVC word+char 83.9% beats the transformer reader's 0.757 on CU stance.
paul_alignment:
Paul's construct-level takeaways are right, and the system has built them. For persona-agency-communion he wanted pre-built codebooks and node design, and the codebook, positive-pole rule and 18-unit test are now in agency_communion_llm.py. The weakness he named, converting a trait into an engine node, is still the open issue. The .60/.40 mapping into susceptibility is not from the paper, persona homophily was unearned (|r| <= 0.015), and the Nokken-drift H4 was below the threshold.

Three of his notes are now stale against the system:
- **LLM readers.** His endorsement of LLM trait reading (llm-and-hybrid-readers) extends the paper beyond its scope. The paper validates sentence-level cue labels, not holistic Big Five item rating, and the Pink reader failed its convergence bar.
- **Gold panels.** The gold-panel note says his notes do not reflect the MISS record. In practice the paper's alpha floor of .70-.78 was what the 2026-07-04 ruling used to set aside the single-rater test.
- **Stance SVM.** His note that 'SVM is outdated' for stance is contradicted by the system's own held-out stance result.

The highlight about role transitions changing displayed personality points to a time-varying persona, which is not built.

extraction.title: Measuring Elite Personality Using Speech
extraction.document_type: Journal article (empirical; measurement method plus validity checks and one substantive application)
extraction.coverage: Full text read: all of _text/5e248be1ab0d.txt (about 1,630 lines; body, footnotes, Tables 1-3, figure notes, references). extraction.research_question: Can Big Five personality traits of US legislators be measured from floor speech text without surveys, and are the resulting estimates valid and substantively useful? Specifically: (a) do text-based estimates parallel known personality-ideology links, (b) do survey nonresponse rates depend on personality, and (c) does Conscientiousness predict the share of symbolic/ceremonial bills proposed, conditional on majority status.
extraction.theory: Big Five (Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, Emotional Stability) personality is related to political behavior and ideology (Gerber et al. 2010, 2011a; Mondak 2010; Jost, Nosek and Gosling 2008). Survey inventories suffer from low response and social desirability, so personality should be inferred from language (Mairesse et al. 2007). Expected ideology signs: Openness, Conscientiousness and Emotional Stability negative toward liberalism; Agreeableness negative to Common Space score; Extraversion agnostic. Symbolic-bill hypothesis: Conscientious legislators propose fewer ceremonial bills because they are goal-oriented and persist against partisan hurdles (Cox and McCubbins 2005; Aldrich 1995); the effect should be larger for the minority, where free-riding on majority leadership is unavailable. Authors also argue Conscientiousness acts as a discount factor (fn 35).
extraction.data: Sources: Congressional Record floor speeches by every sitting House member, 104th-113th Congresses (1996-2014). Unit of measurement: member-year (scores estimated per year, then jackknifed across years). Sample for personality scores: all incumbent House members in the period; the paper does not report total speech counts. Table 1: N = 844 House members (lifetime mean personality, 1996-2014 Common Space). Table 2: NPAT response, N = 598 members (622 in Model 1), pooled by member. Table 3: House bills proposed in 104th-112th Congresses, binomial logit at member-Congress level, N = 3,648 (Models 3-5; 3,736 and 3,732 in Models 1-2). Training data for the pre-trained model: Pennebaker and King (1999) essays (~1.9 million words) and Mehl, Gosling and Pennebaker (2006) conversations (~100,000 words), per Mairesse et al. (2007). Median member uttered ~11,000 words per year (p.7).
extraction.method: Pre-trained Mairesse et al. (2007) SMOreg (SVM regression, Weka) applied to LIWC (2001) and MRCPD features, standardized, in corpus mode: (1) process each member-year's speeches through LIWC and MRCPD; (2) apply the standardized SMOreg models; (3) save Big Five estimates per year; (4) optional jackknife (average of all other years) to reduce language tied to same-year actions; (5) uncertainty from 100 sentence-level bootstrap replications per member-year (Lowe and Benoit 2011), 95% CIs. Scores are on a 1-7 scale and relative to the Congressional Record, not comparable to general-population inventories (fn 10). Validity is indirect: (a) OLS of Common Space scores on lifetime trait means with demographics (Table 1); (b) yearly correlations of traits with LIWC features (Fig 4); (c) authorship/speechwriter checks (Pelosi, Boehner, Ron Paul; p.11); (d) logistic regression of ever responding to NPAT on traits and controls (Table 2, Fig 5); (e) binomial logit of ceremonial-bill share with Majority Party x trait interactions and Congress FE in Model 5 (Table 3, Fig 6). Bill classification follows Volden and Wiseman (2014) title keywords.
extraction.identification: No causal identification strategy. The authors explicitly refrain from claiming causal priority between personality and ideology (fn 20, p.9). Jackknife correction (step 4, p.5) is presented as alleviating endogeneity from same-year action language. The NPAT and bill analyses are conditional associations; the bill model adds party interactions and (Model 5) Congress fixed effects. Selection into survey response is treated as a confound to be shown empirically rather than solved.
extraction.scope: Population: incumbent US House members, 1996-2014 (104th-113th Congress) for personality scores; bill analysis covers House bills in 104th-112th Congresses. Institution: US House floor speech (Congressional Record). Era: post-1996 only; pre-1996 Record not digitized (p.19). Excludes Senate, challengers, state legislators, and presidents (presidents discussed only in an argument, p.11-12). The paper states the method may generalize to other text sources but these are not tested.

summary_md:
Ramey, Klingler and Hollibaugh (PSRM 2016) score Big Five traits for every sitting House member from 1996 to 2014. They run each member-year of Congressional Record floor speech through LIWC and MRC features, then through Mairesse et al.'s pre-trained SMOreg models. Scores sit on a 1-7 scale that is relative to the Record. The method adds an optional leave-one-year-out jackknife and 100 sentence-level bootstrap replications per member-year. Above about 5,000 words a year, confidence intervals narrow to about ±0.15. The paper never validates directly against a personality inventory. Its validity evidence is indirect:
- Lifetime trait means relate to Common Space ideology with the expected signs, but explain only R2 = 0.10 (N = 844).
- Emotional Stability predicts whether a member ever answered the NPAT. Predicted response rises from about 30% to about 53% between -2 SD and +2 SD (N = 598).
- Conscientiousness lowers the share of ceremonial bills a member sponsors (-0.39 to -0.58; N = 3,648 member-Congresses, 104th-112th). A positive Majority × C interaction (+0.27 to +0.29) puts most of that effect in the minority party.

This is the template for Melange's lexical Big Five. fec/members/big5_traits.py names the paper and copies its steps. lep_criterion.py runs the Table 3 ceremonial-share test as its paper-exact C criterion. The test came back null for all three C measures: rho between +0.000 and +0.018, n = 440 members, 115th-118th Congresses pooled, at least 8 sponsored bills each. That run did not split majority from minority, the fault line the paper says carries the effect, so the null is UNSTRATIFIED. The paper also gives no grounds for treating the published RKH scores as ground truth. They come from the same Mairesse-LIWC family, which is why the system's convergence against them is inflated by shared method. Finally, the paper's speechwriter defence covers floor speech only. It does not cover the tweets and interviews the system pools in.

extraction.title: Universal multilayer network exploration by random walk with restart
extraction.document_type: Journal research article (open access, CC BY 4.0), with methods and supplementary material referenced but supplementary notes not in the extracted text
extraction.coverage: Read all 1277 lines of the extracted text (abstract, introduction, results including the RWR formalism, numerical implementation, LOOCV and link-prediction evaluations, parameter-space exploration, discussion, data/code availability, figure captions, references 1-34, back matter). Supplementary Notes 1-5 and Figs S9-S16 are cited but not in the file, so their contents are not covered. Metadata hint corrected: full author list is Anthony Baptista, Aitor Gonzalez, Anais Baudot; article number 170.
extraction.research_question: Can random walk with restart (RWR) be generalized to explore any combination of multiplex, monoplex and bipartite networks (a "universal multilayer network"), and how do added network layers and bipartite links change prediction performance and the stability of outputs to input parameters?
extraction.theory: Random walks as iterative stochastic processes on graphs; RWR as a steady-state diffusion / personalized PageRank measuring proximity of all nodes to seed(s) (p.1-2, citing Lovasz 1993, Brin and Page 1998, Gomez et al. 2013). Multilayer formalism following De Domenico et al. 2013 and Kivela et al. 2014: supra-adjacency matrices for multiplex layers (with inter-layer jump probability delta), bipartite matrices for heterogeneous links, and a column-normalized supra-heterogeneous transition matrix with inter-network jump probabilities lambda and restart parameters eta (network) and tau (layer) (Eqs 5-16, Fig. 2, p.2-4). No behavioural or social theory is used.
extraction.data: Two empirical multilayer networks, no sample sizes given in the main text. (1) Biological network: a gene multiplex (gene physical and functional relationships), a drug multiplex (drug clinical and chemical relationships), and a disease monoplex (phenotypic similarity), linked by gene-disease, drug-gene and drug-disease bipartite networks (p.4, detailed in Supplementary Note 3.B). Unit: genes, drugs, diseases as nodes. (2) Airports network: French, British and German airport multiplex networks (nodes = airports; edges = national flight connections for three airline companies), linked by French-German, British-German and French-British transnational bipartite networks (p.4, Supplementary Note 3.A). Node and edge counts, time period and original sources are not stated in the main text. Data and code are on OSF (doi 10.17605/OSF.IO/ZSMUA) and GitHub (anthbapt/multixrank). Comparison dataset in Methods: the PPI network (p.4-5).
extraction.method: Formal: derivation of RWR on universal multilayer networks (Eqs 1-16), with the normalization generalized from Li and Patra 2010 and Valdeolivas et al. 2018 to N multiplex networks. Implemented as the Python package MultiXrank (optimized, pip installable; complexity analysis in Supplementary Note 2). Evaluation: (a) Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation (LOOCV): each known gene-disease association left out in turn, remaining associations used as seeds, rank of left-out gene recorded and CDF of ranks plotted (p.4-5, Fig. 3a-b). (b) Link Prediction (LP): a gene-disease edge removed and its gene ranked with the disease as seed (p.6, Figs S11, S14). (c) Controls: artificially added transit drug nodes linking gene-disease pairs (1, 2 or 5 per association; Fig 3c-d) and progressive random rewiring of the enhanced bipartite networks (p.5-6). (d) Parameter-space exploration: 125 parameter sets; pairwise similarity of rank output between parameter sets (Eqs 17-18, rank-based distance normalized across multiplex networks), PCA projection, k-means on first two PCs, comparison of top-5 and top-100 nodes per cluster (p.6-8, Fig. 4).
extraction.identification: No causal identification strategy. Predictive performance is assessed against held-out known associations (LOOCV and LP). Causal-style claims about bipartite overlap are made by artificially manipulating bipartite connectivity (transit nodes) and then randomizing edges (p.5-6). Stability of outputs is assessed by varying parameters across 125 sets (p.7).
extraction.scope: Methodological paper. Two example networks only: a biological gene/drug/disease network and a three-country airport network. No population or institution; the airport network is a current-era transport network and the biological network is drawn from unspecified databases. Claims of general applicability (social, economic, ecological networks, p.8) are not tested in the paper.

summary_md:
Baptista, Gonzalez and Baudot (2022) extend random walk with restart (RWR, a seed-personalized PageRank) to "universal" multilayer networks. These combine any number of multiplex networks, where the same nodes appear on several layers, linked by bipartite networks. They build one column-normalized supra-heterogeneous transition matrix with separate dials for layer jumps (delta), jumps between networks (lambda) and restart allocation (eta, tau). The method ships as the MultiXrank Python package.

They test it with leave-one-out ranking (LOOCV) and link prediction on two examples: a gene/drug/disease network and a three-country airport network. In the biological network, adding the drug multiplex did not help. The cause was low bipartite overlap: only 23% of genes and 5% of diseases are shared across the bipartite links. In the airport network, adding the German layer did help, because overlap there is high. Adding artificial transit nodes raised performance, and gradually randomizing those links lowered it again. Across 125 parameter sets, top-ranked outputs were stable in parts of the biological network and very unstable in the airport network.

Three parts of Paul's system are close to this. The staffer network's layer-balanced PageRank already runs a random walk over several layers: each node splits its transition mass equally across its active layers, and teleport is balanced across entity kinds. However, it checks sensitivity only on damping (0.70/0.85/0.95), never on how mass is split across layers. The Congress multilayer builder merges the cosponsor, engagement, HCoI, social and co-appearance layers into a single edge weight, so it has no layer-jump parameter. No held-out test checks whether each added layer improves anything; the only per-layer evidence is null neighbour co-movement on the cosponsor and HCoI layers. The paper's main lesson for this system is to test whether each layer earns its place, and how much its links overlap with the base graph, before treating more layers as more signal. It gives no evidence about legislatures, lobbying or social ties.

extraction.title: Influence maximization in unknown social networks: Learning Policies for Effective Graph Sampling
extraction.venue: AAMAS 2020 (19th International Conference on Autonomous Agents and Multiagent Systems, Auckland); arXiv:1907.11625v5
extraction.document_type: Conference paper (AAMAS 2020, 10 pages), posted to arXiv cs.SI
extraction.coverage: Full text read in one pass: all 981 lines of the 46,239-char text file (front matter, abstract, introduction, problem description, methodology, experiment setup, results, insights, related work, conclusion, references, Tables 1-5). Page images not available, so locations are section names. Paul markup: none (n_annots 0, annot_sha12s empty), so paul_markup is empty and nothing was dropped. Not a Paul research note (no note flag). Metadata corrections: year 2019 is the arXiv posting year and the published year is 2020; venue corrected from arXiv preprint to AAMAS 2020. Paul entry citation (Kamarthi et al. 2020, AAMAS) is consistent with the paper.
extraction.research_question: Can deep reinforcement learning learn a network-discovery (node-querying) policy, under a budget of 5 queries from 5 random seeds, such that the 10 seeds chosen by greedy influence maximization on the discovered subgraph spread further in the full unknown network than the CHANGE sampling heuristic?
extraction.data: Four network families, each split into train and test networks (Table 1). Rural (microfinance diffusion in Indian villages, Banerjee et al. 2013): train rural1, rural2; test rural3, rural4. Animal (vole wildlife contact networks, Davis et al. 2015): train voles1, voles2; test voles3, voles4. Retweet (Twitter retweet networks, Network Data Repository, Rossi and Ahmed 2015): train copen, occupy; test israel (spelled isreal in Table 1), damascus. Homeless (HIV intervention campaigns for homeless youth in Los Angeles, Wilder et al. 2018): train a1, spy, mfp; test b1, cg1, node4, mfp2, mfp3, spy2, spy3. Totals: 9 training networks, 13 test networks. Unit is the network (graph); node counts, edge counts and collection periods are not reported in the text. Synthetic graphs: 5 SBM (or SSM for retweets) graphs per training graph, with Louvain communities. No individual-level sample size is given.
extraction.method: Markov decision process over the discovered subgraph: state is the discovered graph, action is querying an unqueried node, reward is the influence of the final seed set in the full graph at episode end (scaled by Eq. 1 using CHANGE and OPT) plus small per-step rewards for new nodes (Eq. 2). The Geometric-DQN network takes a global graph embedding (GCN layers pooled with DiffPool) plus per-node action embeddings (DeepWalk, found vital for stable training; GCN action features were unstable) and outputs a Q-value per candidate node. Trained with epsilon-greedy DQN, prioritized experience replay and a target network, on a random graph per episode from the training set, with synthetic graphs used on half the episodes. Deployed with frozen weights. Influence oracle: greedy influence maximization on the observed graph (approximating OPT greedily). Diffusion: independent cascade model, p = 0.1, budget 10 activated nodes, T = 5 queries. Baselines: CHANGE (query a random neighbour of each random seed; chosen over random greedy, snowball and recommend, which were 3.9, 42.1 and 41.7 percent worse). Two hand-designed heuristics H1 (query minimum-degree node) and H2 (minimum-degree node among those discovered in the last step) were used for insight analysis.
extraction.identification: Not a causal design. The comparison is algorithmic: policies trained on train networks are evaluated on held-out test networks of the same family, with the same budget, diffusion model and oracle as the baseline. Scores are averages over 100 diffusion simulations. No statistical tests, confidence intervals or seeds-variance reporting appear in the text.
extraction.scope: Social and interaction networks from four domains (rural households, wild voles, Twitter retweets, homeless youth contact networks). Transfer is tested within family only (train on one family's networks, test on that family's held-out networks). Dates of the datasets are not stated. Authors from IIT Madras, McGill University and Mila, and Harvard CRCS. No live field deployment is reported; the paper argues the setting resembles real deployment.
extraction.theory: Independent cascade diffusion (Kempe et al. 2003, 2005) and greedy influence maximization; friendship paradox (Feld 1991) motivates CHANGE; community structure motivates stochastic block models; MDP and POMDP framing for multi-graph training; deep Q-learning with graph representation learning.
extraction.measures: Influence score (mean nodes activated over 100 independent-cascade runs); improve percent (scaled reward: (influence minus CHANGE) divided by (OPT minus CHANGE)); per-step reward; true degree and true betweenness centrality of queried nodes; average improve percent per family.

limitations: OPT is approximated by greedy influence maximization because exact optimization is NP-hard, and the reward depends on CHANGE as the normalizing baseline (Eq. 1).
Table 2 and Table 4 report the best-performing Geometric-DQN variant per test network or test set. The text does not say how the variant was chosen, so these figures may be optimistic.
Environment parameters are fixed (ICM p = 0.1, budget 10, 5 seeds, T = 5 queries); sensitivity to these settings is not reported.
Multi-graph training turns the problem into a POMDP rather than an MDP, which the authors handle by reward scaling without a formal guarantee.
The authors say there is no correlation between performance and discovered graph size, and state that a detailed investigation of the learned patterns is left for future work.
Synthetic-graph results are reported only as a figure with no numbers in the text.
Homeless family is small (3 training and 7 test networks) and the paper gives no node counts or collection periods for any network.
Only the independent cascade model is evaluated; no other diffusion models and no live field deployment are tested.
Text inconsistency: 7-26 percent (Results) vs 7-23 percent (abstract, contributions, conclusion). The paper has no explicit limitations section.

summary_md: Kamarthi, Vijayan, Wilder, Ravindran and Tambe (arXiv 2019, published AAMAS 2020) study influence maximization when the network itself is unknown and must be discovered by querying nodes. Starting from 5 random nodes, an agent gets 5 queries (each reveals a node's neighbours); greedy influence maximization then picks 10 seeds on the discovered subgraph, scored by independent-cascade spread (p = 0.1, 100 runs) on the full graph. Geometric-DQN, a deep Q-network built on a GCN plus DiffPool graph embedding and DeepWalk action embeddings, learns the query policy. Each policy is trained on 9 networks from four families (Indian villages, voles, retweets, homeless youth) and tested on 13 held-out networks from the same families. Against the CHANGE friendship-paradox baseline, the best variant per family improves by 7.91 to 26.6 percent of the gap between CHANGE and greedy-optimal (Table 4). The text quotes this range as 7-23 in some places and 7-26 in others. Reward scaling makes training on several graphs at once possible, and synthetic SBM graphs help. Inspecting the learned policy gives a simple heuristic, H2 (query the lowest-degree node among those just discovered), which beats CHANGE on several test networks. For Paul's systems, the main point is a boundary condition. The cosponsor graph is a fully observed public record. The recruitment and frontier code runs classic greedy on it and states that no ML is needed. The paper's learned policy only pays when edges are hidden. That premise fits the partially observed staffer graph, but only as a way to decide which directories or people to research next. It does not justify any reading of access or influence. The reported numbers pick the best variant per test set and give no confidence intervals.

summary_issues: Training scope is wrong. The summary says each policy is trained on 9 networks pooled across four families. The paper trains and tests per family (Section 4: train and deploy for each network family; Table 1). Each policy sees only its family's 2 or 3 training networks plus synthetic graphs, and is tested on that family's held-out networks.
The summary says the recruitment and frontier code states that no ML is needed. Only the recruitment template comment says this. budget_frontier.py has no such statement.

The summary calls the cosponsor graph a fully observed public record. That is the system's modelling assumption, as the code treats all listed edges as observed. It is not a verified fact about the data and should be labelled as an assumption.

The summary says H2 beats CHANGE on several test networks. That holds for voles3, voles4, damascus and israel. On the Homeless networks the gaps are small (b1 19.4 vs 19.1; spy2 16.4 vs 16.01), and H2 loses on rural3 (17.3 vs 17.4). The summary should not imply broad wins.

gaps_exposed: The cosponsor graph is treated as complete. No component models unobserved ties, or asks how far greedy recruitment and frontier results would move if part of the true contact network is missing from cosponsorship.

The staffer network is admittedly partial (incomplete searches) but has no budgeted policy for which directories or people to resolve next, and no metric for graph completeness after each acquisition round.

The system has not tested whether a cheap structural heuristic (for example H2-style low-degree frontier choice, or degree-ranked seeds) matches lazy greedy on its own kernel P. Such a comparison would show how much the MC-20 greedy machinery buys.
